{{short description|Generalization of signum function to matrices}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''matrix sign function''' is a [[matrix function]] on [[Square matrix|square matrices]] analogous to the complex [[sign function]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Higham|first=Nicholas J.|title=Functions of matrices : theory and computation|date=2008|publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM, 3600 Market Street, Floor 6, Philadelphia, PA 19104)|others=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|isbn=978-0-89871-777-8|location=Philadelphia, Pa.|oclc=693957820|author-link1=Nicholas Higham}}</ref>

It was introduced by J.D. Roberts in 1971 as a tool for model reduction and for solving [[Lyapunov equation|Lyapunov]] and Algebraic [[Algebraic Riccati equation|Riccati]] equation in a technical report of [[Cambridge University]], which was later published in a journal in 1980.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Roberts|first=J. D.|title=Linear model reduction and solution of the algebraic Riccati equation by use of the sign function|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00207178008922881|journal=International Journal of Control|date=October 1980 |language=en|volume=32|issue=4|pages=677–687|doi=10.1080/00207178008922881|issn=0020-7179|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Denman|first1=Eugene D.|last2=Beavers|first2=Alex N.|date=1976|title=The matrix sign function and computations in systems|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0096300376900205|journal=Applied Mathematics and Computation|language=en|volume=2|issue=1|pages=63–94|doi=10.1016/0096-3003(76)90020-5|issn=0096-3003|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Definition ==
The matrix sign function is a generalization of the complex [[Sign function|signum function]]

<math>
 \operatorname{csgn}(z)= \begin{cases}
 1 & \text{if } \mathrm{Re}(z) > 0, \\
 -1 & \text{if } \mathrm{Re}(z) < 0,
\end{cases}
</math>

to the matrix valued analogue <math>\operatorname{csgn}(A)</math>. Although the sign function is not [[Analytic function|analytic]], the [[matrix function]] is well defined for all matrices that have no [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] on the [[imaginary axis]], see for example the [[Analytic function of a matrix#Jordan decomposition|Jordan-form-based definition]] (where the derivatives are all zero).

== Properties ==
'''Theorem:''' Let <math>A\in\C^{n\times n}</math>, then <math>\operatorname{csgn}(A)^2 = I</math>.<ref name=":0" />

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>A\in\C^{n\times n}</math>, then <math>\operatorname{csgn}(A)</math> is [[Diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]] and has eigenvalues that are <math>\pm 1</math>.<ref name=":0" />

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>A\in\C^{n\times n}</math>, then <math>(I+\operatorname{csgn}(A))/2</math> is a [[Projection (linear algebra)|projector]] onto the [[invariant subspace]] associated with the eigenvalues in the [[Right half-plane|right-half plane]], and analogously for <math>(I-\operatorname{csgn}(A))/2</math> and the [[left-half plane]].<ref name=":0" />

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>A\in\C^{n\times n}</math>, and <math>A = P\begin{bmatrix}J_+ & 0 \\ 0 & J_-\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}</math> be a [[Jordan normal form|Jordan decomposition]] such that <math>J_+</math> corresponds to eigenvalues with positive real part and <math>J_-</math> to eigenvalue with negative real part. Then <math>\operatorname{csgn}(A) = P\begin{bmatrix}I_+ & 0 \\ 0 & -I_-\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}</math>, where <math>I_+</math> and <math>I_-</math> are [[Identity matrix|identity matrices]] of sizes corresponding to <math>J_+</math> and <math>J_-</math>, respectively.<ref name=":0" />

== Computational methods ==
The function can be computed with generic methods for [[matrix function]]s, but there are also specialized methods.

=== Newton iteration ===
The [[Newton's method|Newton iteration]] can be derived by observing that <math>\operatorname{csgn}(x) = \sqrt{x^2}/x</math>, which in terms of matrices can be written as <math>\operatorname{csgn}(A) = A^{-1}\sqrt{A^2}</math>, where we use the [[matrix square root]]. If we apply the [[Square root of a matrix#By the Babylonian method|Babylonian method]] to compute the square root of the matrix <math>A^2</math>, that is, the iteration <math display="inline">X_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left(X_k + A^{2} X_k^{-1}\right)</math>, and define the new iterate <math>Z_k = A^{-1}X_k</math>, we arrive at the iteration

<math>
Z_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(Z_k + Z_k^{-1}\right)
</math>,

where typically <math>Z_0=A</math>. Convergence is global, and locally it is quadratic.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

The Newton iteration uses the explicit inverse of the iterates <math>Z_k</math>.

=== Newton–Schulz iteration ===
To avoid the need of an explicit inverse used in the Newton iteration, the inverse can be approximated with one step of the [[Newton's method#Multiplicative inverses of numbers and power series|Newton iteration for the inverse]], <math>Z_k^{-1}\approx Z_k\left(2I-Z_k^2\right)</math>, derived by [[Günther Schulz (mathematician)|Schulz]]([[:de:Günther Schulz (Mathematiker)|de]]) in 1933.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Schulz|first=Günther|date=1933|title=Iterative Berechung der reziproken Matrix|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/zamm.19330130111|journal=ZAMM - Journal of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics / Zeitschrift für Angewandte Mathematik und Mechanik|language=en|volume=13|issue=1|pages=57–59|doi=10.1002/zamm.19330130111|bibcode=1933ZaMM...13...57S |issn=1521-4001|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Substituting this approximation into the previous method, the new method becomes

<math>
Z_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2}Z_k\left(3I - Z_k^2\right)
</math>.

Convergence is (still) quadratic, but only local (guaranteed for <math>\|I-A^2\|<1</math>).<ref name=":0" />

== Applications ==

=== Solutions of Sylvester equations ===
'''Theorem:<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />''' Let <math>A,B,C\in\R^{n\times n}</math> and assume that <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are [[Stable matrix|stable]], then the unique solution to the [[Sylvester equation]], <math>AX +XB = C</math>, is given by <math>X</math> such that

<math>
\begin{bmatrix}
-I &2X\\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}
=
\operatorname{csgn}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
A &-C\\ 0 & -B
\end{bmatrix}
\right).
</math>

''Proof sketch:'' The result follows from the similarity transform

<math>
\begin{bmatrix}
A &-C\\ 0 & -B
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
I & X \\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
A & 0\\ 0 & -B
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
I & X \\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}^{-1},
</math>

since

<math>
\operatorname{csgn}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
A &-C\\ 0 & -B
\end{bmatrix}
\right)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
I & X \\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
I & 0\\ 0 & -I
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
I & -X \\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix},
</math>

due to the stability of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.

The theorem is, naturally, also applicable to the [[Lyapunov equation]]. However, due to the structure the Newton iteration simplifies to only involving inverses of <math>A</math> and <math>A^T</math>.

=== Solutions of algebraic Riccati equations ===
There is a similar result applicable to the [[algebraic Riccati equation]], <math>A^H P + P A - P F P + Q = 0 </math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Define <math>V,W\in\Complex^{2n\times n} </math> as

<math>
\begin{bmatrix}
V & W
\end{bmatrix}
=
\operatorname{csgn}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
A^H &Q\\ F & -A
\end{bmatrix}
\right)
-
\begin{bmatrix}
I &0\\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

Under the assumption that <math>F,Q\in\Complex^{n\times n} </math> are [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] and there exists a unique stabilizing solution, in the sense that <math>A-FP </math> is [[Stable matrix|stable]], that solution is given by the [[Overdetermined system|over-determined]], but [[Consistent and inconsistent equations|consistent]], linear system

<math>
VP=-W.
</math>

''Proof sketch:'' The similarity transform

<math>
\begin{bmatrix}
A^H &Q\\ F & -A
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
P & -I \\ I & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
-(A-FP) & -F\\ 0 & (A-FP)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
P & -I \\ I & 0
\end{bmatrix}^{-1},
</math>

and the stability of <math>A-FP </math> implies that

<math>
\left(
\operatorname{csgn}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
A^H &Q\\ F & -A
\end{bmatrix}
\right)
-
\begin{bmatrix}
I &0\\ 0 & I
\end{bmatrix}
\right)
\begin{bmatrix}
X & -I \\ I & 0
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
X & -I\\ I & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & Y \\ 0 & -2I
\end{bmatrix},
</math>

for some matrix <math>Y\in\Complex^{n\times n} </math>.

=== Computations of matrix square-root ===
The [[Square root of a matrix#By Denman–Beavers iteration|Denman–Beavers iteration]] for the square root of a matrix can be derived from the Newton iteration for the matrix sign function by noticing that <math>A - PIP=0</math> is a degenerate [[algebraic Riccati equation]]<ref name=":2" /> and by definition a solution <math>P</math> is the square root of <math>A</math>.
